question: What does the software development life cycle (SDLC) describe?
correct: The stages a project moves through, from requirements to maintenance
incorrect: The order in which Python executes the lines of a program
How long a computer lasts before it needs replacing
The steps a compiler takes to turn code into machine instructions
feedback: The stages are requirements, design, build, test, deploy, and maintain. Beginners think the whole job is the build stage, which is exactly how avoidable bugs reach real users.

question: Match each SDLC stage to what happens in it.

pairs.definition: Decide what the software must do, and for whom
Decide how it will work: structure, pieces, data
Check that it does what was specified, correctly
Fix bugs and adapt as needs change after release

feedback: It is called a life cycle, not a life line: maintenance turns up new requirements and the loop begins again. Software is never really finished.

question: A hospital app logs a 5.0 mg dose where 0.5 mg was intended. Nobody mistyped anything — the program did it. Which stages failed?
correct: Requirements and test: nobody wrote down the rules for a valid dose, and nobody checked a bad one
incorrect: Deploy and maintain: the release was pushed out too quickly
Design and build: the code was written in the wrong language
Neither: the code ran without crashing, so the process worked
feedback: The code ran perfectly. It was simply wrong. A bug caught at the requirements stage costs a sentence to fix; the same bug caught in a patient's chart costs far more.

question: What is the defining difference between waterfall and agile?
correct: Waterfall runs the stages as one long pass; agile runs them as many short loops
incorrect: Waterfall includes testing while agile skips it to move faster
Waterfall suits small projects and agile suits large ones
Waterfall requires version control while agile does not
feedback: Both cover the same stages. The question is rhythm: one big pass with feedback only at the end, or many small slices with feedback while course corrections are still cheap.

question: What is the main risk of a strict waterfall approach?
correct: You learn whether you built the right thing at the end, when change is costly
incorrect: The team is unable to write documentation along the way
Testing has to happen before the requirements are known
Just one developer is permitted to work at a time
feedback: If nurses first see the app a year in and say that is not how doses are recorded, that is a year of work aimed at the wrong target.

question: In which situation does waterfall still make sense?
correct: Firmware in a medical device, where requirements are fixed and change is costly
incorrect: A new social app where nobody yet knows what users will want
A prototype built to test an idea with a handful of customers
Any project where the team has fewer than five developers
feedback: Waterfall fits when requirements really are fixed, or when a regulator must approve one complete documented package. Most real teams run something agile-ish with as much up-front planning as the risk demands.

question: One short agile cycle, commonly one to four weeks, that ends with working software and user feedback is called a ___.
correct: sprint
feedback: A sprint delivers a thin slice of working software so that what the team learns can change the requirements before the next loop.

question: Which of these is a precise, testable requirement rather than a vague wish?
correct: A recorded dose must be between 0.01 and 1000 mg, or be rejected with an error
incorrect: The app should handle doses sensibly and safely
Dose entry needs to be as fast as the nurses expect
The system should be reliable enough for hospital use
feedback: You can build the first one and later check whether the code obeys it. The other three sound reasonable but give a developer nothing specific to implement or a tester anything to check.

question: Which shape does a user story follow?
correct: As a kind of user, I want some capability, so that some benefit
incorrect: Given some input, when an action happens, the code should not crash
First do this, then do that, and finally save the result
If the condition is true, run this block, otherwise run that one
feedback: The three blanks keep the focus on who needs what and why. The why is what stops a team from building a technically correct feature nobody actually needed.

question: What problem does version control solve?
correct: It records every change so you can see the history and return to an earlier working version
incorrect: It prevents developers from ever writing code that has bugs
It automatically merges two features without any conflicts
It compresses a project so it takes up less space on disk
feedback: It is an unlimited, organised undo across the whole project that never forgets. That is what lets a nervous developer experiment without dread.

question: What is a commit in git?
correct: A saved snapshot of the project at one moment, with a message describing the change
incorrect: A promise to finish a feature before the end of the sprint
A copy of the project uploaded to a teammate's computer
A test that has to pass before the code is permitted to run
feedback: String the commits together and you get the project's history: a timeline you can read, compare, and return to. The message matters — 'fixed the dose validation bug' tells a future teammate why; 'stuff' tells them nothing.

question: Match each git area or command to its role in saving work.

pairs.definition: The files you are currently editing
The changes you have chosen for the next snapshot
Moves a change into the staging area
Saves the staged changes into the history

feedback: The flow is one way: edit, stage what you want, then commit it. Every button in GitHub or a code editor's source-control panel is running these commands underneath.

question: What is a branch used for?
correct: Building a change on a separate timeline without touching the version everyone depends on
incorrect: Storing a backup copy of the project on a second computer
Splitting a large file into smaller files that load faster
Running two versions of the program at the same time
feedback: You can experiment on a branch and break nothing real. When the work is ready, a pull request proposes merging it back into the main line.

question: What happens in a code review?
correct: A teammate reads the proposed changes before they are merged into the main project
incorrect: The author re-reads their own code before committing it
A tool automatically rewrites the code in a standard style
The changes are deployed to users to see if anyone complains
feedback: Review is one of the most important safety nets in software — a second pair of eyes before the code can reach a user. It becomes even more important when an AI wrote the first draft.

question: Which of these are genuine benefits of a project's git history? (Select all that apply)
correct: You can restore a working version after a change breaks something
You can see who changed each line, when, and why
Several people can work in parallel and combine their work
incorrect: Committed code is guaranteed to be free of bugs
The history prevents two people from editing the same file
feedback: Git gives you recovery, an audit trail, and parallel work. It makes no claim about correctness — that is what tests and review are for.

question: What is the central point of the testing section?
correct: Code that runs is not the same as code that is correct
incorrect: Code that runs without an error message is ready to ship
Testing matters chiefly for programs that handle money
A program with no crashes needs no further checking
feedback: The 5.0 mg bug crashed nothing and printed a number. It was simply the wrong number. Testing is how you turn a silent wrong answer into a loud failure.

question: What does the Python statement  assert grams_to_mg(1) == 1000  do?
correct: Nothing if the condition is true; raises an AssertionError and stops if it is false
incorrect: Prints the result of the function so you can read it
Repeats the function call until the condition becomes true
Converts the returned value into the number 1000
feedback: An assert states a fact that must hold if the code is correct. Adding a message after a comma makes the failure describe what went wrong.

question: A function meant to round a dose to one decimal place is written as  return round(mg). Why does  round_dose(0.46)  fail its test?
correct: round(mg) rounds to a whole number, so it returns 0 instead of 0.5
incorrect: round() is unable to accept a value with a decimal point
The function is missing a docstring, so Python refuses to run it
0.46 is below the minimum dose the function is allowed to accept
feedback: The fix is round(mg, 1). This is exactly the flavour of mistake behind the opening disaster: code that runs, looks reasonable, and is quietly wrong.

question: When a change to a program breaks something that used to work, the old bug coming back is called a ___.
correct: regression
feedback: Once a test exists it guards that behaviour forever: if a later change re-breaks it, the test fails again instantly. That is how you catch a regression before a user does.

question: Why do professionals often write the test before writing or fixing the code?
correct: Writing the test forces you to state exactly what correct means first
incorrect: A test written afterwards is unable to detect a failure
Python requires tests to appear above the function they check
Tests run faster when they are written before the code
feedback: The loop is: requirement, test, code, passing test. The test is a precise statement of the requirement, and it keeps guarding that behaviour long after you have moved on.

question: Why should a program's pure logic be separated from its input and output?
correct: Pure logic takes inputs and returns an answer, so it can be checked with assert tests
incorrect: Code that uses print() runs more slowly than code that does not
Python does not allow input() to appear in the same file as a function
Logic and output need separate files for git to track them
feedback: You cannot easily test code that stops to ask a human a question, but you can test a function that takes a secret and a guess and returns two numbers. Designing a testable logic core is what makes the rest of this discipline possible.

question: In AI-assisted development, which task remains the engineer's rather than the AI's?
correct: Decomposing the problem — deciding what pieces should exist and how they fit
incorrect: Writing the body of a clearly described function
Producing a first draft of code quickly
Suggesting names for variables in a finished function
feedback: An AI is very good at filling in a box you have defined. Drawing the boxes — and deciding which of them is testable pure logic — is the engineering job.

question: The notebook says that in AI-assisted work the spec becomes the real artifact you author. Why?
correct: The AI can regenerate code at will; the description of what to build is kept
incorrect: The spec is what the computer actually executes when the program runs
A written spec is required before an assistant will answer
Code written by an AI is barred from a public repository
feedback: A vague request gets vague, buggy code; a precise spec — inputs, rules, edge cases, constraints — gets code worth keeping. Your prompt to an AI is a spec, and writing a good one is the same skill as writing a good requirement.

question: Why is AI-generated code described as plausible rather than correct?
correct: It is produced to read like expert code, which is a separate question
incorrect: It is written in an outdated version of the language
It is correct once the prompt is longer than a paragraph
It runs correctly but is too slow for real programs
feedback: The Wizard is dazzling and confident, and behind the curtain is just a machine pulling levers. Plausible output can hide off-by-one errors, invented functions, or a rule you forgot to state.

question: Which of these are real risks when accepting AI-generated code without review? (Select all that apply)
correct: A subtle logic bug that looks perfectly normal on the page
A call to a library function that does not actually exist
Behaviour that works but violates a rule such as patient privacy
incorrect: The code refuses to run until a human has approved it
The assistant permanently deletes the code you already wrote
feedback: A confident invented function is a hallucination. The privacy case is the important one: no test would have caught it, because it takes a human who knows the organisation's rules and values.

question: An AI writes a function that prints a warning when a dose is out of range but then saves the dose anyway. What kind of problem is this, and what would have caught it?
correct: A correctness bug, which an assert test for an out-of-range dose would have caught
incorrect: A privacy problem, which a human reviewer would have caught
A performance problem, which a timing measurement would have caught
A style problem, which an automatic formatter would have caught
feedback: Printing a warning and continuing is not rejecting. The function should stop — for example by raising an error — so a bad dose is never recorded, and a test asserting that 5000 mg is refused would have found it instantly.

question: The same AI-written function writes the patient's name into a file named public_dose_log.txt. Why is this problem different from the dose bug?
correct: No test would flag it — catching it takes a human who understands the hospital's rules
incorrect: It is not really a problem, since the file is just a log
It would cause the program to crash the first time it ran
It can be fixed automatically by renaming the file
feedback: Even if every line worked exactly as written, dumping identifiable patient data into a shared file is a serious violation. Some flaws tests catch; others only a responsible person can.

question: According to the notebook, what does more AI-written code mean for planning, version control, and testing?
correct: They matter more, since the human's role shifts to being accountable
incorrect: They matter less, since the AI already checks its own output
They matter the same, since the code is identical either way
They become optional once the tests were also written by AI
feedback: That is the throughline of the whole notebook. The human stopped being the one who types and became the one who is responsible.

question: How does the prompt-review-fix loop of AI-assisted work relate to agile?
correct: It is the same build-a-little, check it, adjust cycle, shrunk from weeks to minutes
incorrect: It replaces agile, since feedback from users is no longer needed
It is the opposite of agile, because the whole program is written at once
It has no relationship, since agile applies to teams of people
feedback: Every prompt-review-fix round is a tiny sprint, with you playing the customer who gives feedback. And each loop still needs tests to tell whether the new draft is actually better.

question: Write the Python statement that checks the variable  x  equals 4, stopping the program if it does not.
correct: assert x == 4
feedback: assert states a fact that must be true. Note the double equals: a single = would be an assignment, not a comparison.

question: In AI-assisted work, the precise description of what to build — the artifact you author and keep, while the code is downstream — is called the ___.
correct: spec
feedback: A vague request gets vague, buggy code; a precise spec gets code worth keeping. Your prompt to an AI is a spec, and writing a good one is the same skill as writing a good requirement.
